draft.title: Self-concept
card: Self-concept is how a person sees themselves: their abilities, qualities, roles and worth. It is the picture a person holds of who they are.
It is built partly from a person's own experiences, such as succeeding at a task, failing at one, or trying something new.
It is also built from how others treat them. Praise, criticism, trust and being left out can all shape how a person sees themselves.
Self-concept can change over time. New experiences and new relationships can strengthen it or alter it.
draft.remember: Self-concept is the view you hold of yourself, shaped by what you live through and how others treat you.

a.q: Which of these best describes a person's self-concept?
opts: The view they hold of their own abilities and worth
The opinion their classmates hold about them
The rules their community expects them to follow
The group of people they spend most time with
a.why: Self-concept is the person's own picture of themselves. Other people's opinions can help shape it, but the opinion others hold is not the same as the view the person holds.
a.clue: Whose view of the person is it?

b.q: Lena is new to a school in Wagga Wagga. Her teacher often praises her writing, and she wins a short story prize. She starts to describe herself as a good writer. What does this show?
opts: Self-concept is shaped by experiences and by how others treat us
Self-concept is fixed in childhood and cannot change
Self-concept comes only from a person's own experiences
Self-concept depends only on the opinions of other people
b.why: Lena's prize is her own experience and the teacher's praise is how another person treats her. Together they shaped how she sees herself. The option about only one source is tempting, but the card says both sources help build self-concept.
b.clue: Look for both a personal experience and the treatment from another person.
